after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−7x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=−7y(t)
c
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)
d
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=−7y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must also approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1>0 and λ2>0 is the following: {x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)

content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/aaeba63f6237121fe226eb30e5378d3e93129bb2782b9c8acb8d73ac719676b3.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)
b
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)
c
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)
d
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−y(t)y′(t)=−4y(t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1>0 and λ2<0 is the following: {x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)

content.knowledge_point: Identifying the System Given a Phase Portrait
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/aaeba63f6237121fe226eb30e5378d3e93129bb2782b9c8acb8d73ac719676b3.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

a
{x′(t)=5x(t)y′(t)=−2y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
c
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)

{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
e
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)

decision.explanation: Arrows along both axes point toward the origin, so both coefficients must be negative. Option b has solutions x(t)=C₁e^{-2t} and y(t)=C₂e^{-5t}, with trajectories y=C|x|^{5/2} matching the displayed stable node.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/039bae0d2eedf7d12d8283b2b134855c531efcba1bd0fa14fe9f841b28d5204e.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=5x(t)y′(t)=−2y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
c
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
d
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
e
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ1<0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must also approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1<0 and λ2<0 is the following: {x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)

content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−6x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=−6y(t)
c
{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
d
{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−6x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: The arrows point toward the origin along both axes, requiring both coefficients to be negative. Option a gives x(t)=C₁e^{-6t} and y(t)=C₂e^{-3t}; its trajectories y=C|x|^{1/2} approach the origin tangent to the y-axis, matching the portrait.
